id_tips: High-elevation fir with flat needles, two white bands underneath, and upright purple cones. Needles are blunt and fragrant when crushed. Bark on young trees is smooth gray with resin blisters.
habitat: Spruce-fir forest on the highest Southern Appalachian peaks, generally above about 5,500 ft. Cool, wet, acidic soils.
wnc: A Southern Appalachian endemic. Best stands are on Mount Mitchell, the Black Mountains, Grandfather Mountain, and the Great Smokies. Wild trees have been devastated by the balsam woolly adelgid.
uses: North Carolina's signature Christmas tree and the state's most important Christmas-tree crop because of needle retention and scent. In the wild it is cover and seed for high-elevation birds (including the spruce-fir specialist birds of the Black Mountains). Wood is light and not a major timber species.
caution: Wild high-elevation stands are a rare, declining ecosystem. Do not harvest wild trees.
lookalikes: Red spruce has four-sided, sharp needles that roll in the fingers; Fraser fir needles are flat and will not roll.
wikipedia_extract: Abies fraseri, commonly known as Fraser's fir, or Fraser fir, is an endangered species of fir in the order Pinales native to the Appalachian Mountains of the southeastern United States. It is endemic to the Appalachian Mountains, where it grows in 48 populations on seven montane regions in the range.

id_tips: Evergreen with short, flat needles (about 1/2 inch) with two white lines beneath and a tiny extra needle lying along the twig. Cones are small (1/2–1 inch) and hang from the tips. Feathery, drooping branchlets.
habitat: Cool ravines, stream banks, north slopes, and coves from low mountains to about 5,000 ft.
wnc: A signature tree of WNC gorges and old-growth coves. Hemlock woolly adelgid has killed huge numbers; surviving trees are often treated in parks.
uses: Bark was a major historical source of tannin for leather. Wood is used for pulp and rough construction. Living trees shade trout streams and keep water cold. Not related to poison hemlock (an herb).
caution: Needles and tea from this tree are not the same as poison hemlock, but do not confuse names. Adelgid-killed snags can drop limbs.
lookalikes: Carolina hemlock has longer needles that radiate all around the twig rather than lying flat. Fraser fir grows much higher and has upright cones.

Tsuga canadensis, also known as Canadian hemlock, eastern hemlock-spruce, or eastern hemlock, and in the French-speaking regions of Canada as pruche du Canada, is a coniferous tree in the pine family, Pinaceae, native to eastern North America. It is the state tree of Pennsylvania. Eastern hemlocks are widespread throughout much of the Great Lakes region, the Appalachian Mountains, The Maritimes and the Northeastern United States. They have been introduced in the United Kingdom and mainland Europe, where they are used as ornamental trees.
Eastern hemlock populations in North America are threatened in much of their range by the spread of the invasive Hemlock woolly adelgid, which infests and eventually kills trees. Declines in population from hemlock wooly adelgid infestation have led to Tsuga canadensis being listed as Near Threatened on the IUCN Red List.
Eastern hemlocks are long lived

id_tips: Needles are longer than eastern hemlock (about 1/2–3/4 inch) and stick out all around the twig instead of lying in a flat spray. Cones are larger, 1–1.5 inches.
habitat: Dry rocky ridges, bluffs, and gorges; a Southern Appalachian specialty.
wnc: Much less common than eastern hemlock. Look on exposed rock outcrops in the Blue Ridge. Also attacked by hemlock woolly adelgid.
uses: Limited timber use. Important as a rare endemic of dry mountain rock habitats and as a garden evergreen.
caution: Same adelgid threat as eastern hemlock.
lookalikes: Eastern hemlock needles look two-ranked and flatter on the twig.
wikipedia_extract: Tsuga caroliniana, the Carolina hemlock, is a species of conifer in the pine family, Pinaceae, endemic to the southern Appalachian Mountains of the United States.  As of 2023, it is under review for listing under the Endangered Species Act of 1973.

id_tips: Needles are four-sided, sharp, and roll between the fingers. Cones hang down and are 1–2 inches. Bark is reddish-brown and scaly.
habitat: High peaks with Fraser fir, generally above 4,500–5,000 ft in WNC.
wnc: Defines the spruce-fir zone with Fraser fir. A northern tree that survives as a sky-island population on southern peaks.
uses: Historically used for paper pulp, sounding boards in musical instruments, and construction. Wildlife cover at elevation. Not a major WNC timber tree today.
caution: High-elevation habitat is sensitive; stay on trails.
lookalikes: Fraser fir needles are flat and blunt, with white stomatal bands below.
wikipedia_extract: Picea rubens, commonly known as red spruce, is a species of spruce native to eastern North America, ranging from Nova Scotia to eastern Quebec and south-eastern Ontario, and south through the Adirondack Mountains and New England along the Appalachians to western North Carolina and eastern Tennessee. This species is also known as yellow spruce, West Virginia spruce, eastern spruce, and he-balsam. Red spruce is the provincial tree of Nova Scotia.

id_tips: The only WNC pine with five needles per bundle. Needles are soft, thin, and bluish-green, 3–5 inches. Long, slender cones (4–8 inches) with unarmed scales.
habitat: Moist to dry mountain slopes, old fields, and mixed forests. Very common in WNC.
wnc: A dominant pine of the mountains. Huge trees remain in Pisgah and the Smokies.
uses: Premier historical mast and lumber tree of eastern North America. Soft, workable wood for interior trim, matches, and construction. Seeds eaten by squirrels, birds, and (in small amounts) people. White-pine needle tea is a traditional vitamin-C drink.
caution: Pine-needle tea is usually made from white pine; do not use yew or unknown evergreens. Pregnant people are often advised to avoid medicinal-strength pine teas.
lookalikes: All other WNC pines have 2 or 3 needles per bundle.

Pinus strobus, commonly called the eastern white pine, northern white pine, white pine, Weymouth pine (British), and soft pine is a large pine native to eastern North America. It occurs from Newfoundland, Canada, west through the Great Lakes region to southeastern Manitoba and Minnesota, United States, and south along the Appalachian Mountains and upper Piedmont to northernmost Georgia and very rare in some of the higher elevations in northeastern Alabama. It is considered rare in Indiana.
The Haudenosaunee maintain the tree as the central symbol of their multinational confederation, calling it the "Tree of Peace", where the Seneca use the name o'sóä' and the Mohawk people call it onerahtase'ko:wa. Within the Wabanaki Confederacy, the Mi'kmaq use the term guow to name the tree, both the Wolastoqewiyik and Peskotomuhkatiyik call it kuw or kuwes, and the Abenaki use the term kowa.

id_tips: Two twisted yellow-green needles per bundle. Cones are heavy, armed with stout hooked spines, and stay on the tree for years. Often a scrubby, crooked tree on rock.
habitat: Dry, fire-prone rocky ridges and outcrops of the Blue Ridge and Appalachians.
wnc: A Southern/Central Appalachian endemic. Look on exposed south-facing rock at middle elevations.
uses: Little commercial timber (form is poor). Cones and habitat are important for ridge wildlife. Needs occasional fire to open serotinous cones and reduce competition.
caution: Spines on cones are sharp.
lookalikes: Pitch pine has 3 needles; Virginia pine has 2 needles but weaker cone prickles and is more weedy.
wikipedia_extract: Table Mountain pine, Pinus pungens, also called hickory pine, prickly pine, or mountain pine, is a small species of conifer in the family Pinaceae, a pine native to the Appalachian Mountains in the United States.

id_tips: Two short, twisted needles per bundle (1.5–3 inches). Small egg-shaped cones with a thin prickle. Often keeps dead lower branches, looking scruffy.
habitat: Dry, poor soils, old fields, and disturbed sites at low to middle elevations.
wnc: A common pioneer pine on worn-out fields and dry ridges in the lower mountains.
uses: Pulpwood, rough lumber, and firewood. Wildlife cover on dry sites. Not a high-value timber tree.
caution: None special.
lookalikes: Table Mountain pine cones are much more heavily armed; shortleaf pine needles are longer and more flexible.

Pinus virginiana, the Virginia pine, scrub pine, Jersey pine, or possum pine, is a medium-sized conifer in the family Pinaceae, a pine often found on poorer soils from Long Island in southern New York south through the Appalachian Mountains to western Tennessee and Alabama. The usual size range for this pine is 5.5 to 18 metres. However, it can grow larger under optimum conditions. The trunk can be as large as 20 inches in diameter. This tree prefers a well-drained loam or clay, but will also grow on substandard, sandy soil, where it remains small and stunted. The typical life span is 65 to 90 years.
The short (4–8 cm), yellow-green needles are paired in fascicles and are often twisted. Pinecones are 4–7 cm long and may persist on the tree for many years, often (though not always) releasing their seeds in the second year. In growth habit, some trees may be inclined with twisted trunks.

id_tips: Two (sometimes 3) slender flexible needles, 3–5 inches. Small prickly cones. Bark on mature trees has resin pockets that look like holes or 'volcanoes' in the plates.
habitat: Dry to moist uplands; more common in the lower mountains and foothills than on high peaks.
wnc: The main yellow pine of the mountain foothills. Less common at high elevation.
uses: Valuable southern yellow-pine lumber and pulp. Wildlife eat the seeds. Historically a major naval-stores and timber species.
caution: None special.
lookalikes: Virginia pine has shorter, more twisted needles and a scruffier form.
wikipedia_extract: The shortleaf pine or Pinus echinata is a species of coniferous tree in the family Pinaceae, a pine endemic to the United States. The shortleaf pine is sometimes referred to as the "old field", "spruce", "rosemary", "yellow", "two-leaf" and "heart" pine. The common name "shortleaf pine" may refer to other species like loblolly pine (Pinus taeda), based on a custom in the Southeastern United States to only refer to pines as either "long-leaf" or "short-leaf". However, P. echinata can be distinguished from other pines by examining its short leaves and small cones.

id_tips: A juniper, not a true cedar. Scale-like adult leaves; sharp needles on young growth. Blue, berry-like cones. Shreddy reddish-brown bark. Often columnar.
habitat: Dry limestone or rocky soils, old fields, fencerows, and roadsides. Full sun.
wnc: Common in pastures and dry openings, especially over mafic or limestone rock.
uses: Aromatic heartwood for chests, closets, fence posts, and pencils (rot-resistant). Blue 'berries' flavor gin and are eaten by cedar waxwings. Traditional cold remedies used the berries; evidence is limited.
caution: Pollen is a major allergen. 'Berries' in quantity can be irritating. Not a food staple.
lookalikes: True cedars (Cedrus) are planted ornamentals and have needle clusters on short shoots.
wikipedia_extract: Juniperus virginiana, also known as eastern red cedar, red cedar, Virginian juniper, eastern juniper, red juniper, and other local names, is a species of juniper native to eastern North America from southeastern Canada to the Gulf of Mexico and east of the Great Plains. Farther west it is replaced by the related Juniperus scopulorum (Rocky Mountain juniper) and to the southwest by Juniperus ashei (Ashe juniper).  It is not to be confused with Thuja occidentalis (eastern white cedar).

id_tips: Leaves are unique: four-lobed, notched at the tip, like a tulip silhouette. Large green-and-orange tulip-like flowers in late spring. Straight trunk with tight diamond-furrowed bark on old trees.
habitat: Cove forests, moist slopes, and old fields. Fast-growing canopy tree.
wnc: One of the tallest eastern hardwoods; cove giants in the Smokies exceed 150 ft. (Tennessee's state tree; NC's state tree is pine.)
uses: Major timber tree (lightweight, stable lumber for furniture, millwork, pallets). A top honey plant; bees make a strong dark honey. Cherokee and settlers used the wood for dugout canoes. Inner bark was a traditional tonic. Seeds feed finches and squirrels.
caution: Not a true poplar. Flowers are not typically eaten.
lookalikes: Nothing else in WNC has the notched four-lobed leaf.

Liriodendron tulipifera—known as the tulip tree, American tulip tree, tulipwood, tuliptree, tulip poplar, whitewood, fiddletree, lynn-tree, hickory-poplar, and yellow-poplar—is the North American representative of the two-species genus Liriodendron (the other member is Liriodendron chinense). It is native to eastern North America from Southern Ontario and possibly southern Quebec west to Illinois, and east to southwestern Massachusetts, then south to central Florida and Louisiana.
The tulip tree is the tallest tree of the Nearctic temperate deciduous forest. It can grow to more than 50 m (160 ft) in virgin cove forests of the Appalachian Mountains, often with no limbs until it reaches 25–30 m (80–100 ft) in height, making it a very valuable timber tree.

habitat: Almost everywhere: swamps, coves, dry ridges, yards. The most widespread tree in eastern North America.
wnc: One of the most common trees at all elevations except the highest fir zone.
uses: Soft-maple lumber and pulp. Can be tapped for syrup, but sugar content is lower than sugar maple. Early flowers are a critical bee food in March. Seeds (samaras) feed squirrels and birds.

Acer rubrum, the red maple, also known as swamp maple, water maple, or soft maple, is one of the most common and widespread deciduous trees of eastern and central North America. The U.S. Forest Service recognizes it as the most abundant native tree in eastern North America. The red maple ranges from southeastern Manitoba around the Lake of the Woods on the border with Ontario and Minnesota, east to Newfoundland, south to Florida, and southwest to East Texas. Many of its features, especially its leaves, are quite variable in form. At maturity, it often attains a height around 30 m (100 ft). Its flowers, petioles, twigs, and seeds are all red to varying degrees. Among these features, however, it is best known for its brilliant deep scarlet foliage in autumn.

wikipedia_extract: Acer saccharum, the sugar maple, is a species of flowering plant in the soapberry and lychee family Sapindaceae. Sugar maple is best known for being the primary source of maple syrup and for its brightly colored autumn foliage. It may also be called "rock maple", "sugar tree", "sweet maple", or, particularly in reference to the wood, "hard maple", "birds-eye maple", or "curly maple", the last two being specially figured lumber.

The striped maple is a sequential hermaphrodite, meaning that it can change its sex throughout its lifetime. It is the only species of snakebark maple native to North America.

habitat: Cool, moist mountain coves, streamheads, and high-elevation hardwoods.

It is one of two beech species native to North America, the other occurring in Mexico. It flourished over most of the continent prior to the last ice age, but is now limited to the east. The tree is shade tolerant and found in forests in the final stage of succession.
The nuts are eaten by animals and humans. The leaves and inner bark can be prepared as well.

habitat: Upland forests, coves, and dry ridges. Long-lived canopy oak.
wnc: A keystone tree of mountain oak forests. Hosts hundreds of moth and butterfly caterpillars.

caution: Raw acorns are bitter and high in tannins; leach before eating. Oak wilt and gypsy/spongy moth can stress trees.

Quercus alba, the white oak, is one of the preeminent hardwoods of eastern and central North America. It is a long-lived oak, native to eastern and central North America and found from Minnesota, Ontario, Quebec, and southern Maine south as far as northern Florida and eastern Texas. Specimens have been documented to be over 450 years old.
Although called a white oak, it is very unusual to find an individual specimen with white bark; the usual color is a light gray. The name comes from the colour of the undersides of the leaves. In the forest it can reach a magnificent height and in the open it develops into a massive broad-topped tree with large branches striking out at wide angles.

id_tips: Leaves with 7–11 bristle-tipped lobes, sinuses cut about halfway to the midrib. Bark of mature trees has smooth, shiny vertical 'ski tracks'. Large bitter acorns with a shallow saucer cap.
habitat: Moist to dry mountain slopes; one of the most common canopy oaks in WNC.
wnc: A workhorse oak from low valleys to high ridges.
uses: Major timber oak (furniture, flooring, railroad ties). Acorns are an important wildlife mast (more tannic than white oak). Hosts a huge number of caterpillars, so it is a top bird tree.
caution: Acorns need thorough leaching if used as food.
lookalikes: Black oak and scarlet oak have deeper sinuses; scarlet oak sinuses cut nearly to the midrib and look like a skeleton leaf.
wikipedia_extract: Quercus rubra, the northern red oak or common red oak, is an oak tree in the red oak group (Quercus section Lobatae). It is a native of North America, in the eastern and central United States and southeast and south-central Canada. It has been introduced to small areas in Western Europe, where it can frequently be seen cultivated in gardens and parks. It prefers good soil that is slightly acidic. Often simply called red oak, northern red oak is so named to distinguish it from southern red oak (Q. falcata), also known as the Spanish oak.

id_tips: Leaves look like American chestnut: oblong with rounded, wavy teeth, not deep lobes, and no bristle tips. Bark is dark, thick, and deeply ridged. Large acorns.
habitat: Dry, rocky ridges and south slopes — the classic ridge oak of the Blue Ridge.
wnc: Dominates many dry WNC ridge forests, often with mountain laurel and sourwood.
uses: High-tannin bark was used for leather tanning. Heavy wood for ties and construction. Large acorns are important wildlife food.
caution: Do not confuse with American chestnut, which has sharper teeth and long catkins of nuts in very spiny burs.
lookalikes: American chestnut leaves are more sharply toothed and the tree is now almost only a sprout shrub. White oak is more deeply lobed.
wikipedia_extract: Quercus montana, the chestnut oak, is a species of oak in the white oak group, Quercus sect. Quercus. It is native to the eastern United States, where it is one of the most important ridgetop trees from southern Maine southwest to central Mississippi, with an outlying northwestern population in southern Michigan. It is also sometimes called rock oak because of its presence in montane and other rocky habitats.

id_tips: Usually 5 (sometimes 7) smooth leaflets. Tight bark, not shaggy. Nuts are pear-shaped with a thin husk that only partly splits; kernels are often bitter.
habitat: Dry to moist upland forests, very common in the mountains and Piedmont.
wnc: One of the most common hickories on WNC slopes.
uses: Excellent firewood (high heat). Tool handles and sporting goods from springy wood. Wildlife eat the nuts; people usually prefer shagbark or mockernut.
caution: Hickory husks can stain. Nuts may be bitter.
lookalikes: Mockernut has 7–9 densely hairy leaflets. Shagbark has peeling vertical bark plates.
wikipedia_extract: Carya glabra, the pignut hickory, is a common, but not abundant species of hickory in the oak-hickory forest association in the Eastern United States and Canada. Other common names are pignut, sweet pignut, coast pignut hickory, smoothbark hickory, swamp hickory, and broom hickory. The pear-shaped nut ripens in September and October, has a sweet maple like smell, and is an important part of the diet of many wild animals. The wood is used for a variety of products, including fuel for home heating. It has pinnately compound leaves that turn a golden yellow in the fall.

id_tips: Bark peels in long, loose vertical plates — the shaggy look. Usually 5 large leaflets. Sweet, thick-shelled nuts in a four-split husk.
habitat: Rich woods, coves, and bottomlands. Less common on dry ridges than pignut.
wnc: Present in richer mountain forests; not as ubiquitous as pignut.
uses: The best native hickory nut for people. Wood for tool handles, smoking meat, and firewood. Squirrels cache the nuts.
caution: Nut shells are very hard; watch your fingers.
lookalikes: Shellbark hickory (Carya laciniosa) is similar but rarer here and usually has 7 leaflets and a larger nut.
wikipedia_extract: Carya ovata, the shagbark hickory, is a common hickory native to eastern North America, with two varieties. The trees can grow to quite a large size but are unreliable in their fruit output. The nut is consumed by wildlife and historically by Native Americans, who also used the wood.

id_tips: Alternate simple leaves, finely toothed, with two small glands on the leaf stalk. Mature bark is dark and flaky like burnt potato chips. Long hanging clusters of white flowers, then dark cherries.
habitat: Cove forests, roadsides, old fields, and mixed woods. Fast-growing.
wnc: Common from valleys to high coves. One of the first trees to color (yellow-orange) in late summer.
uses: One of the most valuable Appalachian cabinet woods (red-brown heartwood). Ripe fruit for jelly, wine, and wildlife. Bark was the traditional 'wild cherry bark' cough syrup (contains cyanogenic compounds — not a DIY medicine).
caution: Wilted leaves, bark, and seeds contain cyanide-releasing compounds and can kill livestock. Fruit pulp is edible when fully ripe; spit out the pits.
lookalikes: Sweet birch bark can look similar when young; scrape a twig — cherry is bitter-almond, birch is wintergreen.

id_tips: Finely toothed sour-tasting leaves. Midsummer sprays of white, urn-shaped flowers that look like lily-of-the-valley. Deeply furrowed gray bark. Brilliant scarlet fall color, often the first tree to turn.
habitat: Acidic upland woods, oak-heath ridges, and road banks.
wnc: A Southern Appalachian signature. Sourwood honey is a famous WNC product.
uses: Sourwood honey is one of the most prized honeys in the United States — light, complex, and made when almost nothing else is blooming in late June–July. Leaves were chewed as a thirst quencher. Wood is hard and used for tool handles and pulp. Excellent ornamental.
caution: Leaves taste sour from oxalic acid; do not eat large amounts. Not a maple; no syrup.
lookalikes: Flowering sprays and sour leaves are distinctive. Blackgum has untoothed leaves and blue fruit.
wikipedia_extract: Oxydendrum arboreum ( OK-sih-DEN-drəm ar-BOR-ee-əm), commonly known as sourwood or sorrel tree, is the sole species in the genus Oxydendrum, in the family Ericaceae. It is native to eastern North America, from southern Pennsylvania south to northwest Florida and west to southern Illinois; it is most common in the lower chain of the Appalachian Mountains. The tree is frequently seen as a component of oak-heath forests.

id_tips: Opposite leaves with veins that curve to follow the margin. Spring 'flowers' are four white (or pink) bracts around a cluster of tiny true flowers. Alligator-skin bark on older trunks. Shiny red berries in fall.
habitat: Understory of hardwood forests, roadsides, and yards.
wnc: North Carolina's state flower (the blossom). Still common but hit hard by dogwood anthracnose in cool, wet mountain sites.
uses: Hard wood for shuttles, mallets, and golf-club heads historically. Berries are a top fall food for migrating birds (not tasty to people). A premier native ornamental. Traditional bark teas were used for fever; they are not a safe home medicine.
caution: Berries can upset human stomachs. Anthracnose is worse in dense shade; trees do better with some sun and air flow.
lookalikes: Kousa dogwood (Asian ornamental) has pointed bracts and raspberry-like fruit. Pagoda dogwood has alternate leaves.
wikipedia_extract: Cornus florida, the flowering dogwood or American dogwood, is a species of flowering tree in the family Cornaceae native to eastern North America and northern Mexico. The tree is commonly planted as an ornamental in residential and public areas because of its showy bracts and interesting bark structure.

id_tips: Heart-shaped leaves, smooth-edged. Magenta-pink pea flowers bloom on bare twigs and even on old trunks in early spring, before leaves. Flat pea-like pods later.
habitat: Forest edges, rich woods, roadsides, and yards. Lower to middle elevations.
wnc: Common in the lower mountains and foothills; less so on the coldest peaks.
uses: Flowers are edible — tart, pea-like — in salads. A nitrogen-fixing legume that improves soil. Excellent early nectar for bees. Premier native ornamental.
caution: Eat only the flowers in moderation; pods are not a food crop.
lookalikes: Nothing else in WNC blooms magenta right on the bark in March–April.
wikipedia_extract: Cercis canadensis, the eastern redbud, is a large deciduous shrub or small tree, native to eastern North America from southern Michigan south to central Mexico, west to New Mexico, but able to thrive as far west as California and as far north as southern Ontario. It is the state tree of Oklahoma and the official city tree of Huntington Beach. The prevalence of the so-called "Columbus strain" has seen the residents of Columbus, Wisconsin, embrace the plant in their city's identity. Known as the "Redbud City," the town hosts "Redbud Day" annually the Saturday before Mother's Day, organizing a variety of themed events to recognize the tree.

id_tips: Small tree. Five-petaled white flowers in early spring, often before or with the first leaves. Leaves finely toothed. Fruit looks like a small purple apple/blueberry. Smooth gray bark with faint stripes.
habitat: Woods, edges, and rocky slopes. One of the first trees to bloom.
wnc: Very common. 'Sarvis' in Appalachian speech. Several Amelanchier species overlap in the mountains.
uses: Ripe fruit is edible and excellent — like a blueberry-almond cross — for people, birds, and bears. Early bloom is important for native bees. Wood is hard but small.
caution: Pits are small; fruit is eaten whole like blueberries. Confirm ID; some rose-family lookalikes are less tasty.
lookalikes: Hawthorns have thorns and tougher fruit. Dogwood blooms later with four bracts, not five petals.
wikipedia_extract:
Amelanchier arborea (downy serviceberry or common serviceberry), is a small tree native to eastern North America from the Gulf Coast north to Thunder Bay in Ontario and Lake St. John in Quebec, and west to Texas and Minnesota.
Other common names are "shadberries" (as their blossoming coincides with the shad runs in New England), "Juneberries" (because the berries usually set on in June), and "Service" or "Sarvice" berries because their blooms mean that the muddy back roads into the "coves and hollers" of Appalachia will soon be passable for circuit-riding preachers and the communities will be able to have Sunday services again. (Some say, more morbidly, that it means the ground is soft enough to dig, which means that those who died over winter can be buried and have services said over them.)

id_tips: Leaves come in three shapes on the same tree: oval, mitten (1 lobe), and 3-lobed. Crushed leaves and roots smell of root beer. Green twigs. Small yellow flowers; dark blue fruit on red stalks.
habitat: Old fields, roadsides, and woodland edges. Often clonal thickets from root sprouts.
wnc: Common at low to middle elevations, especially on disturbed ground.
uses: Dried powdered leaves are filé, the thickener in gumbo. Historically the root was the original root-beer flavor. Fruit feeds birds. Wood is light and aromatic. A spicebush-swallowtail host plant.
caution: Safrole in the root oil is a listed carcinogen in high doses; the FDA banned safrole as a food additive. Occasional filé (leaves) is the traditional culinary use; do not make homemade sassafras oil or drink strong root teas.
lookalikes: The three leaf shapes plus root-beer smell are diagnostic.

caution: Berries are poisonous to people and pets (vomiting, diarrhea). Leaves are not edible.

habitat: Upland woods to wet flats; very adaptable.

id_tips: Opposite palmate leaves with 5 (sometimes 7) large leaflets. Smooth to lightly plated gray bark. Yellow flower panicles in spring. Large shiny buckeye nuts in a leathery husk.
habitat: Rich, moist cove forests — a hallmark of the best Southern Appalachian coves.
wnc: One of the trees that makes WNC cove forests famous. Often with silverbell, basswood, and sugar maple.
uses: Native people leached the toxic nuts to make them edible — a laborious process, not recommended. Wood is soft (sometimes used for pulp or crates). A superb native shade tree. Nuts are a curiosity, not a snack.
caution: All parts, especially nuts and young shoots, contain aesculin and are poisonous to people and livestock if eaten raw.
lookalikes: Ohio buckeye (rare here) has spiny husks and a foul odor when twigs are crushed. Horsechestnut is a planted European tree with sticky buds.
wikipedia_extract: Aesculus flava, also known commonly as the common buckeye, the sweet buckeye, and the yellow buckeye, is a species of deciduous tree in the subfamily Hippocastanoideae of the family Sapindaceae. The species is native to the Ohio Valley and Appalachian Mountains of the Eastern United States. It grows in mesophytic forests or floodplains, generally in acidic to circumneutral soil, reaching a height of 20 to 48 m (66 to 157 ft).

habitat: Rich coves and moist mountain slopes.
wnc: A Southern Appalachian characteristic tree. Huge specimens grow in Great Smoky Mountains coves.
uses: Primarily an ornamental and cove-forest tree. Flowers feed bees. Little commercial timber. One of the plants that tells you that you are in a rich mountain cove.
caution: None special.
lookalikes: Flowering dogwood has four bracts, not hanging bells. Sourwood flowers are later and urn-shaped on the twig tips.

habitat: Rich coves and moist slopes.
wnc: The common large magnolia of WNC coves. Fraser and umbrella magnolias are smaller understory trees with bigger leaves.
uses: Soft wood similar to tuliptree, used for furniture and pallets. A native ornamental. Seeds eaten by birds and small mammals.
caution: None special.
lookalikes: Fraser magnolia leaves have ear-like lobes at the base. Umbrella magnolia leaves are huge and clustered in umbrellas at the twig tips.
wikipedia_extract:
Magnolia acuminata, commonly called the cucumber tree (often spelled as a single word "cucumbertree"), cucumber magnolia or blue magnolia, is one of the largest magnolias, and one of the cold-hardiest. It is a large forest tree of the Eastern United States and Southern Ontario in Canada. It is a tree that tends to occur singly as scattered specimens, rather than in groves.
The cucumber tree is native primarily within the Appalachian belt, including the Allegheny Plateau and Cumberland Plateau, up to western Pennsylvania and New York. There are also numerous disconnected outlying populations through much of the southeastern U.S., and a few small populations in Southern Ontario. In Canada, the cucumber tree is listed as an endangered species and is protected under the Canadian Species at Risk Act. id_tips: Large leaves with two ear-like lobes (auricles) at the base. Creamy-white fragrant flowers. Understory or midstory tree of mountain coves.
habitat: Moist mountain forests, especially coves and north slopes.
wnc: A Southern Appalachian specialty, common along WNC hiking trails.
uses: Ornamental native. Flowers are a spring nectar source. Little timber use (usually too small and poorly formed).
caution: None special.
lookalikes: Umbrella magnolia lacks the ear lobes. Cucumber magnolia is a much larger tree with unlobed leaves.
wikipedia_extract: Magnolia fraseri, commonly known as Fraser's magnolia, Fraser magnolia, mountain magnolia, earleaf cucumbertree, or mountain-oread, is a species of magnolia native to the southeastern United States in the southern Appalachian Mountains and adjacent Atlantic and Gulf Coastal Plain from West Virginia to northern Florida and to eastern Texas. The Appalachian plants are classified as Magnolia fraseri var. fraseri, and the more coastal plants as M. fraseri var. pyramidata. These two kinds of magnolia are sometimes recognized as distinct species, M. fraseri and M. pyramidata, respectively.

id_tips: Large, tropical-looking simple leaves in a drooping fan. Deep maroon, three-petaled flowers in spring before or as leaves emerge. Fruit is a green, mango-sized cluster that ripens to yellow-brown in early fall.
habitat: Rich, moist bottomlands, cove toes, and stream terraces. Often in clonal patches.
wnc: Common in lower-elevation rich woods; less so on high, cold ridges.
uses: Largest edible fruit native to the United States — creamy, banana-mango flavor when fully ripe and soft. Host plant for the zebra swallowtail. Traditional food of Native peoples and settlers.
caution: Eat only fully ripe fruit; unripe fruit and seeds are irritating. Some people get a skin rash from handling fruit (pawpaw is related to poisonwood/custard-apples). Do not eat seeds or leaves.
lookalikes: Young magnolias have large leaves but very different flowers and no banana-scented fruit.
wikipedia_extract:
Asimina triloba, the American papaw, pawpaw, paw paw, or paw-paw, among many regional names, is a species of small deciduous tree. It has large leaves and produces a large, yellowish-green to brown fruit.
The species is native to eastern North America, in a more temperate range than its tropical relatives. It is a patch-forming (clonal) understory tree of hardwood forests, being found in well-drained, deep, fertile bottomland and also hilly upland habitat.
Although much of the plant contains the neurotoxin annonacin, the ripe fruits are edible. They are sweet, with a custard-like texture and a flavor somewhat similar to banana or pineapple. They are commonly eaten raw, but are also used to make ice cream and baked desserts.
image_credit: Photo via Wikipedia / Wikimedia Commons (File:Asimina_triloba3.jpg). Used for local study.

id_tips: Blocky, charcoal-like bark in square plates. Alternate untoothed leaves. Female trees bear orange fruit the size of a small tomato. Unripe fruit is fiercely astringent.
habitat: Old fields, dry woods, roadsides, and bottomland edges. Lower to middle elevations.
wnc: Common in the lower mountains. A classic Appalachian fruit tree.
uses: Fruit is excellent after frost or when fully soft-ripe — pudding, bread, wildlife forage (opossums, foxes, people). Very hard wood (ebony family) for golf-club heads, shuttles, and tools. Male and female flowers on separate trees.
caution: Unripe persimmons are so astringent they can cause serious mouth puckering; wait until they are jelly-soft. Large amounts of unripe fruit can cause bezoars (stomach blockages) in rare cases.
lookalikes: Blackgum has similar blocky bark but blue fruit and usually a more horizontal branching pattern.

Diospyros virginiana is a persimmon species commonly called the American persimmon, common persimmon, eastern persimmon, simmon, possumwood, possum apples,  or sugar plum. The tree is typically dioecious, so one must have both male and female plants to obtain fruit.
It ranges from southern Connecticut to Florida, and  west to Texas, Louisiana, Oklahoma, Kansas, and Iowa. The tree grows in the wild but has been cultivated for its fruit and wood since prehistoric times by Native Americans. Both the tree and the fruit are referred to as persimmons, with the latter appearing in desserts and cuisine in the U.S. South and Midwest.

wikipedia_extract: Carpinus caroliniana, the  American hornbeam, is a small hardwood understory tree in the genus Carpinus. American hornbeam is also known as blue-beech, ironwood, musclewood and muscle beech for the distinctive sinewy, muscle-like appearance of its trunk. It is native to eastern North America, from Minnesota to southern Quebec, east to Maine, and south to eastern Texas and northern Florida. It occurs in shaded areas with moist soil, particularly near the banks of streams or rivers, and is often a natural understory species of the riverine and maritime forests of eastern temperate North America.

Platanus occidentalis, also known as American sycamore or American planetree, is a species of Platanus native to the eastern and central United States, the mountains of northeastern Mexico, extreme southern Ontario, and extreme southern Quebec. It is usually called sycamore in North America, a name which can refer to other types of trees in other parts of the world; in the United Kingdom, for example, the name sycamore typically refers to Acer pseudoplatanus. The American sycamore is a long-lived species, typically surviving at least 200 years and likely as long as 500–600 years. It is capable of becoming a massive tree, with a wide girth and heights reaching up to 24 m (80 ft) or more.
The species epithet occidentalis is Latin for "western", referring to the Western Hemisphere, because at the time when it was named by Carl Linnaeus, the only other species in the genus was P. orientalis

habitat: Rich coves, bottomlands, and old farmsteads.
wnc: Common in fertile valleys and coves; a farm-tree classic.

Juglans nigra, the eastern American black walnut, is a species of deciduous tree in the walnut family, Juglandaceae, native to central and eastern North America, growing mostly in riparian zones.
Black walnut is an important tree commercially, as the wood is a deep brown color and easily worked. Walnut seeds (nuts) are cultivated for their distinctive and desirable taste. Walnut trees are grown for lumber and food, and processors have found additional markets for even the tough outer hulls by finely grinding them for use in products such as abrasive cleansers. Many cultivars have been developed for improved quality wood or nuts. In 2017, the United States Department of Agriculture valued U.S. walnut timber at $530 billion. A significant amount is grown in Missouri.

id_tips: Pinnate leaves with 7–19 oval leaflets. Paired spines at nodes on young growth. Hanging white, fragrant pea-flower clusters in May. Flat brown pods. Deeply furrowed, ropey bark.
habitat: Native to the Southern Appalachians; now widely naturalized on roadsides, old fields, and mines.
wnc: Truly native here (this is part of its original range) but aggressive on disturbed ground.
uses: Exceptionally rot-resistant wood for fence posts, decks, and firewood (very high heat). A major honey plant (black-locust honey). Nitrogen fixer that builds soil on stripped land. Flowers are edible in fritters.
caution: Bark, leaves, and especially seeds are toxic to people and livestock (toxalbumins). Eat only the flowers, cooked, in moderation. Spines are stout.
lookalikes: Honey locust has branched thorns on the trunk and smaller leaflets. Mimosa (invasive) has pink powder-puff flowers and twice-compound leaves.

Robinia pseudoacacia, commonly known as black locust, is a medium-sized hardwood deciduous tree, belonging to the tribe Robinieae of the legume family. Another common name is false acacia, a literal translation of the specific name (pseudo [Greek ψευδο-] meaning 'fake' or 'false' and acacia referring to the genus of plants with the same name).
Although fossilized traces of the genus were found in Europe, the species itself is native to a few small areas of the United States, but has been widely planted and naturalized elsewhere, including temperate North America, Eurasia, and Africa. It is considered an invasive species in some regions.

id_tips: Today almost always a multi-stem sprout from an old root system, rarely over 20 ft before blight kills it back. Leaves are long, lance-shaped, with sharp forward-pointing teeth and a pale underside. Long catkins in early summer. Very spiny burs with 2–3 nuts (when a tree flowers).
habitat: Was the dominant canopy tree of Appalachian forests. Sprouts persist in oak-chestnut ridges.
wnc: The great lost tree of these mountains. Blight (Cryphonectria parasitica) arrived in the early 1900s. Restoration hybrids and blight-resistant work are ongoing.
uses: Historically the most important wildlife and human nut tree in the East — sweet nuts, rot-resistant timber, tannin, and mast that fattened hogs and bears. That economy collapsed with the blight.
caution: Do not confuse with horsechestnut (toxic) or Chinese chestnut (planted, usually a rounder leaf). Leave rare flowering stems alone if they are part of restoration.
lookalikes: Chestnut oak has wavy rounded teeth, not sharp. Chinese chestnut leaves are often thicker and hairier.

The American chestnut (Castanea dentata) is a large, fast-growing deciduous tree of the beech family native to eastern North America. As is true of all species in the genus Castanea, the American chestnut produces burred fruit with edible nuts. The American chestnut was once common in the Appalachian Mountain range and was a dominant species in the oak-chestnut forest region of its central and southern range.
During the early to mid-20th century, American chestnut trees were devastated by chestnut blight, a fungal disease that came from Japanese chestnut trees that were introduced into North America from Japan. It is estimated that the blight killed between three and four billion American chestnut trees in the first half of the 20th century, beginning in 1904. Four mature American chestnuts exist within its former range, although many stumps and root systems continue to send up saplings.

id_tips: Heart-shaped, coarsely toothed leaves, often lopsided at the base. Flowers and nutlets hang from a leafy wing-like bract. Often sprouts a ring of stems around an old stump.
habitat: Rich coves and north slopes. A cove-forest indicator with buckeye and silverbell.
wnc: Common in the best mountain coves. White basswood (T. americana var. heterophylla) with silvery leaf undersides is the southern mountain form.
uses: A legendary honey tree (linden honey). Soft, even wood for carving, boxes, and Native American basswood-fiber cordage from the inner bark. Flowers have a traditional calming tea use in Europe (same genus).
caution: None special. Some people are sensitive to linden tea.
lookalikes: Red mulberry has similar leaves but milky sap and different fruit. Basswood leaves are not milky.
wikipedia_extract: Tilia americana is a species of tree in the family Malvaceae. It is native to eastern North America, from southeast Manitoba east to New Brunswick, southwest to northeast Oklahoma, southeast to South Carolina, and west along the Niobrara River to Cherry County, Nebraska. It is the sole representative of its genus in the Western Hemisphere, assuming T. caroliniana is treated as a subspecies or local ecotype of T. americana. Common names include American basswood and American linden.

id_tips: Opposite pinnate leaves, usually 7 leaflets, pale beneath. Diamond-furrowed bark. Paddle-shaped single-winged seeds (samaras). Winter buds are chocolate-brown.
habitat: Rich coves, well-drained woods, and old fields.
wnc: Once common; emerald ash borer has killed most mature ashes in the region. Standing dead ash is now a familiar (and dangerous) sight.
uses: The classic baseball-bat, tool-handle, and furniture wood — strong and springy. Seeds feed birds. A host of many insects, which is why the borer is so destructive.
caution: Dead ash trees drop large limbs without warning. Do not picnic under them.
lookalikes: Green ash leaflets are greener beneath and more toothed; both are dying from the same beetle. Boxelder (a maple) has similar opposite compound leaves but green twigs and paired maple seeds.

Fraxinus americana, the white ash or American ash, is a fast-growing species of ash tree native to eastern and central North America. The tree is highly valued as lumber.
The white ash population in North America is being devastated by the invasive emerald ash borer, which has already killed hundreds of millions of them as it spreads, starting in during the 1990s. Billions more are expected to die by 2050. Surviving white ashes are often much younger, with the oldest and tallest white ashes largely becoming dead trees due to the emerald ash borer.
image_credit: Photo via Wikipedia / Wikimedia Commons (File:Fraxinus_americana_002.jpg). Used for local study.

id_tips: Evergreen shrub. Leathery oval leaves. Clusters of white-to-pink flowers with unique pentagon-pocketed corollas in late spring. Twisted trunks in dense 'laurel hells'.
habitat: Acidic oak-heath forests, rocky slopes, and stream gorges. Very common.
wnc: A defining shrub of the Blue Ridge. 'Ivy' in local speech often means this or rhododendron.
uses: Premier native ornamental. Dense thickets are wildlife cover. Hard wood was used for spoons and tool handles. Flowers are pollinated by bumblebees in a spring-loaded anther mechanism.
caution: All parts are highly toxic (grayanotoxins). Honey from mountain laurel/rhododendron can cause 'mad honey' poisoning. Never make tea from the leaves.
lookalikes: Rhododendron maximum has much larger leaves and larger, more open flowers. Sheep laurel (Kalmia angustifolia) is a smaller shrub with narrower leaves.
wikipedia_extract: Kalmia latifolia, the mountain laurel, calico-bush, or spoonwood, is a flowering plant and one of the 10 species in the genus of Kalmia belonging to the heath(er) family Ericaceae. It is native to the eastern United States. Its range stretches from southern Maine to northern Florida, and west to Indiana and Louisiana. Mountain laurel is the state flower of Connecticut and Pennsylvania. It is the namesake of Laurel County in Kentucky, the city of Laurel, Mississippi, Mount Laurel, New Jersey, and the Laurel Highlands in southwestern Pennsylvania.

caution: All parts toxic (grayanotoxins). Do not ingest leaves, flowers, or honey made purely from rhododendron.

Rhododendron catawbiense, with common names Catawba rosebay, Catawba rhododendron, mountain rosebay, purple ivy, purple laurel, purple rhododendron, red laurel, rosebay, rosebay laurel, is a species of Rhododendron native to the eastern United States, growing mainly in the southern Appalachian Mountains from West Virginia south to northern Alabama.
It is a dense, suckering shrub growing to 3 m (9.8 ft) tall, rarely 5 m (16 ft). The leaves are evergreen, 6–12 cm (2.4–4.7 in) long and 2–4 cm (0.79–1.57 in) broad. The flowers are 3–4.5 cm (1.2–1.8 in) in diameter, violet-purple, often with small spots or streaks, blooming from April through June. The fruit is a dry capsule 15–20 mm (19⁄32–25⁄32 in) long, containing numerous small seeds.
The species is named after the Catawba River.

wikipedia_extract: Rhododendron calendulaceum, the flame azalea, is a species of Rhododendron. It is a deciduous shrub that grows up to 120–450 cm tall. This species of Rhododendron is native to the Appalachian Mountains in the eastern United States, ranging from southern Pennsylvania and Ohio to northern Georgia. It may be extirpated from Pennsylvania and Alabama. It occurs naturally in mixed deciduous forests and is typically found in woodland slopes and mountain balds in the Appalachians, where it prefers dry and rocky mountain woods. The inflorescences of Rhododendron calendulaceum are visited by many animals such as bees, butterflies, hummingbirds and small mammals. It is a popular cultivated plant due to its bright yellow, orange or red flowers.

wnc: A classic Southern Appalachian native shrub, widely planted.

wikipedia_extract: Calycanthus floridus, or commonly known as the eastern sweetshrub, Carolina allspice, or spicebush, is a species of flowering shrub in the family Calycanthaceae. It is identifiable by its dark red flowers and fragrant scent. It is non-invasive and is found in the Southeastern United States. The Nature Conservancy considers its conservation status to be G5, globally secure, indicating it is at low risk of extinction.

wnc: Wild blueberries are a mountain tradition. Lowbush species (V. pallidum and others) are even more common on dry ridges.

caution: Confirm you have a Vaccinium; some other white-berried or red-berried heaths are not blueberries. Avoid roadsides that may be sprayed.

habitat: Ditches, wet fields, creek edges, and forest openings.
wnc: Common in valleys and damp roadsides. (Now often treated as Sambucus nigra subsp. canadensis.)
uses: Ripe cooked berries for jelly, syrup, and wine. Flowers for fritters and tea. A traditional cold-and-flu folk remedy (evidence is mixed; commercial extracts exist). Wildlife devour the fruit. Stems were used for spiles and whistles.
caution: Bark, leaves, stems, roots, and unripe berries contain cyanogenic glycosides and should not be eaten. Ripe berries should be cooked. Do not make homemade medicinal doses for children.

Sambucus canadensis, the American black elderberry, Canada elderberry, or common elderberry, is a New World species of elderberry that forms a shrub primarily in temperate regions.
Most parts of the plant are toxic with cyanogenic glycosides, but the ripe berries can be cooked for food use with the seeds removed.

id_tips: Herbaceous vine with three-lobed leaves and tendrils. Elaborate purple-and-white flowers with a fringe (corona). Egg-shaped green fruit (maypops) that wrinkle and turn yellowish when ripe.
habitat: Sunny fields, roadsides, and garden edges. Lower elevations.

habitat: Woods, fencerows, and floodplains.

uses: Native hummingbird vine and ornamental. Can be used as a native substitute for invasive climbing hydrangea or English ivy on supports.

Bignonia capreolata is a vine commonly referred to as crossvine.  The common name refers to the cross-shaped pattern revealed when the stem is cut; this pattern results from four radial wedges of phloem embedded within the stem's xylem.  It is native to the central and southern United States.  The vine climbs without twining but does produce tendrils.  It produces long tubular flowers which are red and yellow and frequently have a mocha fragrance.  The leaves are dark green to almost purple and produced as opposite pairs with terminal tendrils.  The vine often climbs very high, with leaves only remaining on the uppermost portion of the plant. Crossvine can spread aggressively through stolons and may need to be managed in garden or domestic settings.

Trillium grandiflorum, the white trillium, large-flowered trillium, great white trillium, white wake-robin or in French: trille blanc, is a species of flowering plant in the family Melanthiaceae. A monocotyledonous, herbaceous perennial, the plant is native to eastern North America, from northern Quebec to the southern parts of the United States through the Appalachian Mountains into northernmost Georgia and west to Minnesota. There are also several isolated populations in Nova Scotia, Maine, southern Illinois, and Iowa.
Trillium grandiflorum is most common in rich, mixed upland forests. It is easily recognized by its attractive three-petalled white flowers, opening from late spring to early summer, that rise above a whorl of three leaf-like bracts. It is an example of a spring ephemeral, a plant whose life-cycle is synchronized with that of the deciduous woodland which it favours.

wnc: Common in sunny, well-drained sites in the lower mountains.
uses: A top monarch and native-bee plant. Traditional 'pleurisy root' medicine is unsafe by modern standards. Beautiful native perennial.
caution: Milkweeds are toxic if eaten (cardiac glycosides). Do not ingest. This species is the least milky but still not a food.
lookalikes: Common milkweed has dusty-pink balls of flowers and milky sap. Jewelweed is orange but has hanging spotted flowers and watery stems.
wikipedia_extract: Asclepias tuberosa, commonly known as butterfly weed or pleurisy root, is a species of milkweed native to eastern and southwestern North America. It is commonly known as butterfly weed because of the butterflies that are attracted to the plant by its color and its copious production of nectar.
image_credit: Photo via Wikipedia / Wikimedia Commons (File:Asclepias_tuberosa_interior.jpg). Used for local study.

id_tips: Towering 5–10 ft perennial. Whorled leaves. Dome of dusty-pink flower heads in late summer. Stems are hollow and often purple-spotted.
habitat: Ditches, wet meadows, and creek edges.
wnc: A late-summer giant of WNC roadsides. Several Eutrochium species occur here.
uses: A magnet for swallowtails, bees, and monarchs. Traditional fever herb (Joe Pye is a folk figure); not a proven modern medicine. Excellent native garden plant for wet sun.
caution: None special. Not a food.
lookalikes: Ironweed has deeper purple, tighter heads and alternate (not whorled) leaves. Spotted Joe-Pye (E. maculatum) is similar; hollow-stem is the common big one in the south.
wikipedia_extract:
Eutrochium fistulosum (Eupatorium fistulosum), also called hollow Joe-Pye weed, trumpetweed, or  purple thoroughwort, is a perennial North American flowering plant in the family Asteraceae. It is native to southern Canada and throughout the eastern and south central United States from Maine west to Ontario, Wisconsin, and Missouri and south as far as Florida and Texas. The specific name fistulosum refers to the tubular stem; see fistula.
Eutrochium fistulosum is a herbaceous perennial plant sometimes as much as 350 cm (140 in; 11 ft 6 in) tall. It is found in moist, rich soil alongside ditches and marshes, or in wet forests. It flowers from mid-summer to the first frosts, makes an attractive backdrop in garden plots, and is very attractive to butterflies, bees, and other nectar-feeding insects. In addition, it is a larval host to the Clymene moth, eupatorium borer moth, ruby tiger moth,

id_tips: Brilliant scarlet five-petaled flowers, each petal notched. Sticky stems. Blooms in late spring on banks and open woods.
habitat: Rocky woods, road banks, and woodland edges.
wnc: A hummingbird wildflower of WNC spring.
uses: Native ornamental and hummingbird plant. Not a food or medicine plant of any importance.
caution: None special.
lookalikes: Cardinal flower is taller and later. Indian pink (Spigelia) has a yellow-lined red tube and is less common here.
wikipedia_extract: Silene virginica, the fire pink, is a perennial wildflower native to eastern and central North America that belongs to the pink family, Caryophyllaceae. Fire pink, known for its distinct, brilliant-red flowers, begins blooming in late spring and stays in bloom throughout the summer.
image_credit: Photo via Wikipedia / Wikimedia Commons.

id_tips: Evergreen, round, glossy, toothed leaves in a groundcover mat; they bronze in winter. A wand of tiny white flowers in late spring.
habitat: Acidic mountain woods, often under rhododendron and oak.
wnc: A Southern Appalachian endemic-centered species. Leaves were (and sometimes still are) harvested for the florist trade.
uses: Florist greenery. A beautiful native groundcover for shade. Not edible.
caution: Commercial wild-harvest of leaves can damage populations; buy cultivated or leave it.
lookalikes: Oconee bells (Shortia) has similar rounded leaves but notched petals and a much narrower range. Wild ginger leaves are duller and heart-shaped.
wikipedia_extract: Galax, the wandplant, wandflower, or beetleweed, is a genus in the flowering plant family Diapensiaceae, containing a single species, Galax urceolata (syn. G. rotundifolia, G. aphylla). It is native to the southeastern United States from Massachusetts and New York south to northern Alabama, growing mainly in the Appalachian Mountains at altitudes of up to 1,500 m, where it grows in shaded places in forests. Galax urceolata can occur at multiple ploidy levels, an individual may be a diploid (2x), triploid (3x), or autotetraploid (4x) (autopolyploid). The cytotypes are neither morphologically nor geographically distinct, though there are slight climatic differences between the diploid and autotetraploid types. Outcrossing is likely to occur among cytotypes as well.
image_credit: Photo via Wikipedia / Wikimedia Commons (File:Galax_urceolata.jpg). Used for local study.

id_tips: Succulent stems. Orange, hanging, spotted flowers with a spur. Seed pods explode when touched. Pale jewelweed (I. pallida) is yellow and also common in WNC.
habitat: Wet woods, seeps, creek edges, and ditches.
wnc: A summer weed of every wet trail.
uses: The classic folk poultice for poison ivy and nettle stings (crush the watery stems and rub on). Studies are mixed; many hikers still swear by it. Young shoots have been cooked as a green. Hummingbirds use the flowers. Seeds are edible and walnut-flavored.
caution: Eating large amounts raw is unwise (it can be irritating). Test a small amount of juice on skin if you have sensitive skin.
lookalikes: Spotted jewelweed is orange; pale jewelweed is lemon-yellow and prefers slightly cooler coves.
wikipedia_extract: Impatiens capensis, the orange jewelweed, common jewelweed, spotted jewelweed,  jewelweed, spotted touch-me-not, or orange balsam, is an annual plant in the family Balsaminaceae that is native to North America. It is common in bottomland soils, ditches, and along creeks, often growing side by side with its less common relative, yellow jewelweed (I. pallida).
image_credit: Photo via Wikipedia / Wikimedia Commons (File:2016-07-07 14 31 30 Jewelweed with purple tinted leaves along U.S. Route 50 (Northwestern Pike) in far eastern Hampshire County, West Virginia.jpg). Used for local study.

id_tips: Tall, rank herb with magenta-red stems. Alternate leaves. Long clusters of white flowers then dark purple berries with red stalks. Perennial root is huge.
habitat: Disturbed ground, edges, gardens, and floodplains.
wnc: A common native 'weed' of farmsteads and woods edges.
uses: Young spring shoots are the traditional 'poke sallet', boiled in several changes of water — a risky folk food. Berries yield a magenta dye and feed birds. The plant is being studied for antivirals; that is not a home use.
caution: Roots, mature leaves, seeds, and raw berries are poisonous (phytolaccatoxin). Children have been poisoned eating berries. Do not eat poke unless you have expert traditional training — and even then many toxicologists say skip it.
lookalikes: Elderberry has opposite compound leaves, not alternate simple leaves on red stems.
wikipedia_extract:
Phytolacca americana, also known as American pokeweed, pokeweed, polk salad, poke sallet, pokeberry, dragonberries, pigeonberry weed, and inkberry, is a poisonous, herbaceous, perennial plant in the pokeweed family Phytolaccaceae. This pokeweed grows 1 to 3 metres (4 to 10 ft). It has simple leaves on green to red or purplish stems and a large, white taproot. id_tips: Hairy stems and leaves. Yellow daisy flowers with a dark brown central cone. Blooms all summer in sun.
habitat: Fields, roadsides, and open woods.
wnc: Common. Cutleaf coneflower (R. laciniata) is the tall streamside cousin.
uses: Native pollinator plant and cheerful ornamental. Not a significant food plant. A traditional Native dye and mild medicinal; evidence is limited.
caution: None special.
lookalikes: Orange coneflower (R. fulgida) is similar. False sunflower and other yellow daisies lack the dark raised cone.
wikipedia_extract: Rudbeckia hirta, commonly called black-eyed Susan and yellow coneflower, is a North American flowering plant in the family Asteraceae. It grows to 1 metre (3+1⁄2 ft) tall with daisy-like yellow flower heads. There are numerous cultivars. It was used medicinally by Native Americans and is the state flower of Maryland.
image_credit: Photo via Wikipedia / Wikimedia Commons (File:Rudbeckia_hirta_kz03.jpg). Used for local study.

id_tips: Nodding red-and-yellow flowers with five long spurs. Lacy, three-part compound leaves. Blooms in spring on rocks and banks.
habitat: Rocky woods, cliffs, and road cuts.
wnc: Common on Blue Ridge rock outcrops.
uses: Hummingbird and native-bee plant. Native ornamental. Seeds were a traditional medicine; the genus contains toxic alkaloids.
caution: Do not eat. Garden columbines hybridize with it if planted nearby.
lookalikes: Garden columbines are often blue, pink, or purple and more upright.
wikipedia_extract: Aquilegia canadensis, the Canadian columbine, Canada columbine, eastern red columbine, or wild columbine, is a species of flowering plant in the buttercup family. It is a perennial plant that is native to the woodlands and rocky areas in eastern North America in both the United States and southern Canada. It readily hybridizes with other plants in the columbine genus and is a common garden plant.
image_credit: Photo via Wikipedia / Wikimedia Commons (File:Wild_Columbine.jpg). Used for local study.

id_tips: Evergreen, round, glossy, galax-like leaves with toothed edges. White to pale-pink flowers with five notched petals in early spring. Low groundcover of rich gorges.
habitat: Very local: moist, acidic gorges in a small Southern Appalachian range (Jocassee / Keowee / some NC sites).
wnc: A rare Southern Appalachian endemic, famous among botanists. Many historic sites were flooded by reservoirs. Do not collect.
uses: A conservation flagship and garden plant from nursery stock only. No food use.
caution: Rare. Photograph and leave it. Never dig wild plants.
lookalikes: Galax is much more common, with a wand of many tiny flowers rather than a few larger notched bells.
wikipedia_extract: Shortia galacifolia, the Oconee bell is a rare North American plant in the family Diapensiaceae found in the southern Appalachian Mountains, concentrated in the tri-state border region of Georgia, North Carolina, and South Carolina. Additional populations (some of them naturalized) have been found in Alabama, Tennessee, Virginia, and Massachusetts. Shortia  galacifolia has also been reported in Japan, as have three other species of Shortia.
image_credit: Photo via Wikipedia / Wikimedia Commons (File:Shortia_galacifolia_-_2013.jpg). Used for local study.

id_tips: Creeping evergreen with paired, white-veined round leaves. Twin white tubular flowers fuse to make one red berry with two 'eyes' (the leftover calyxes).
habitat: Acid woods, often on mossy banks and under pines and oaks.
wnc: A common native groundcover on WNC trails.
uses: Edible but bland, seedy berries — a nibble, not a crop. Traditional women's herbal (not validated; name is outdated). Excellent native groundcover.
caution: Do not use as a homemade pregnancy herb.
lookalikes: Wintergreen (Gaultheria) has minty leaves and berries at the leaf axils, not twin flowers.
wikipedia_extract: Mitchella repens (commonly partridge berry or squaw vine) is the best known plant in the genus Mitchella. It is a creeping prostrate herbaceous woody shrub occurring in North America belonging to the madder family (Rubiaceae).
image_credit: Photo via Wikipedia / Wikimedia Commons (File:Mitchella_repens_Partridge_berry_Norfolk_Connecticut_05112019.jpg). Used for local study.

id_tips: Low evergreen of the forest floor. Glossy oval leaves that smell strongly of wintergreen when crushed. White urn flowers, then red berries that last into winter.
habitat: Acidic oak, pine, and mountain woods.
wnc: Common on dry to moist acidic slopes.
uses: Leaves and berries are edible and taste like teaberry gum (the original flavor). Traditional tea. Oil of wintergreen (methyl salicylate) was distilled from this and from sweet birch.
caution: Concentrated wintergreen oil is extremely toxic (it is essentially a liquid aspirin relative). A few milliliters can kill a child. Enjoy a leaf or berry; never make or swallow the oil.
lookalikes: Partridgeberry has paired white-veined leaves and no minty scent.
wikipedia_extract: Gaultheria procumbens, also called the eastern teaberry, the checkerberry, the boxberry, or the American wintergreen, is a perennial species of Gaultheria native to northeastern North America from Newfoundland west to southeastern Manitoba, and south to Alabama. It is a member of the Ericaceae (heath family).
image_credit: Photo via Wikipedia / Wikimedia Commons (File:Gaultheria_procumbens.JPG). Used for local study.

id_tips: Pair of heart-shaped, deciduous, slightly hairy leaves. A hidden brown-maroon jug flower at ground level in spring. Rhizome smells of ginger. Evergreen Hexastylis ('little brown jugs') is the more common WNC relative.
habitat: Rich deciduous woods.
wnc: Asarum canadense is in the mountains; several Hexastylis species (little brown jugs) are even more typical of WNC acid woods.
uses: Rhizome was a ginger substitute and traditional medicine. A native groundcover. Pipevine swallowtails sometimes use related plants.
caution: Contains aristolochic acids, which are kidney-toxic and carcinogenic. Do not eat wild ginger as a regular food or tea. Use culinary ginger instead.
lookalikes: Hexastylis species have thicker, often mottled evergreen leaves and similar hidden jug flowers.
wikipedia_extract:
Asarum canadense, commonly known as Canada wild ginger, Canadian snakeroot, Indian Ginger, Coltsfoot, and Broad-Leaved Asarabacca, is a herbaceous, perennial plant. It should not be confused for Asarum reflexum, a closely related species, or Asarum acuminatum, a variety of A. canadense.
It forms dense colonies in the understory of deciduous forests throughout its native range in eastern North America. It is protected as a threatened species in Maine due to habitat loss. The species has been used by Native Americans for cooking and medicine, although recent research has suggested that compounds within the plant could cause negative health problems.
image_credit: Photo via Wikipedia / Wikimedia Commons (File:Asarum_canadense_-_Wild_Ginger.jpg). Used for local study.

id_tips: Evergreen fern. Each leaflet (pinna) has a little thumblike lobe at the base, like a Christmas stocking. Fertile fronds have smaller, spore-covered leaflets toward the tip.
habitat: Wooded slopes, almost any forest that is not a bog.
wnc: The default evergreen fern of WNC woods.
uses: Native evergreen groundcover. Traditional Christmas greenery. Not edible (most ferns are not; some fiddleheads of other species are eaten with caveats).
caution: Do not assume any fiddlehead is edible. Christmas fern is a landscape plant, not a food.
lookalikes: Holly ferns and wood ferns lack the stocking-thumb on every pinna.
wikipedia_extract: Polystichum acrostichoides, commonly denominated Christmas fern, is a perennial, evergreen fern native to eastern North America, from Nova Scotia west to Minnesota and south to Florida and eastern Texas. It is one of the most common ferns in eastern North America, being found in moist and shady habitats in woodlands, stream banks and rocky slopes. The common name derives from the evergreen fronds, which are often still green at Christmas.

id_tips: Big vase-shaped fern of wet ground. Separate cinnamon-brown fertile fronds stand in the center in spring; green sterile fronds surround them. Woolly cinnamon tufts at the base of pinnae.
habitat: Seeps, bogs, wet woods, and ditch edges.
wnc: Common in mountain seeps. Interrupted fern is a close cousin of drier slopes.
uses: Ornamental native of wet gardens. Fiddleheads are sometimes listed as edible but are not a recommended wild food (and cinnamon fern is often confused with other osmundas).
caution: Skip the fiddleheads. Many ferns contain carcinogens if eaten regularly.
lookalikes: Interrupted fern has brown spore segments in the middle of an otherwise green frond. Royal fern looks more like a locust leaf and grows in wetter spots.

Osmundastrum cinnamomeum, commonly known as the cinnamon fern or the buckhorn fern, is a species of royal fern native to the Americas and Asia. It is the sole living representative of the genus Osmundastrum, which was separated from Osmunda after modern phylogenetic studies demonstrated that Osmunda was not monophyletic. In North America it occurs from southern Labrador west to Ontario, and south through the eastern United States to eastern Mexico and the West Indies; in South America it occurs west to Peru and south to Paraguay. In Asia it occurs from southeastern Siberia south through Japan, Korea, China and Taiwan to India, Myanmar, Thailand and Vietnam.
Osmundastrum cinnamomeum has a fossil record extending into the Late Cretaceous of North America, approximately 73 million years ago, making it one of the oldest living plant species. The genus itself goes back to the Triassic.

id_tips: Shiny black, wiry stems. Fronds split into a fingered horseshoe of delicate green leaflets. Looks nothing like Christmas fern.
habitat: Rich, moist, rocky woods and cove slopes.
wnc: A hallmark of fertile mountain coves.
uses: Beloved native ornamental for shade. Traditional hair and respiratory folk uses are not modern medical recommendations.
caution: None special. Do not wild-collect for gardens; buy nursery plants.
lookalikes: Unmistakable among WNC ferns once you see the black stems and circular frond.
wikipedia_extract: Adiantum pedatum, the northern maidenhair fern, is a species of fern in the family Pteridaceae, native to moist forests in eastern North America. Like other ferns in the genus, the name maidenhair refers to the slender, shining black stipes. Taxonomy classification disputes occur due to the distribution of A. Pedatum in both North America and East Asia.

id_tips: Fast-growing tree with long pinnate leaves (11–41 leaflets). Each leaflet has a small glandular tooth near the base. Crushed leaves and male flowers smell like rancid peanut butter. Smooth bark becoming lightly striped.
habitat: Roadsides, city lots, forest edges, and disturbed woods. Originally from China.
wnc: Listed by NC Forest Service and NC-IPC as a high-threat invasive in the mountains. Preferred host of the spotted lanternfly.
uses: None recommended in North America. Historically planted as a tough urban tree. In its native range it has medicinal and wood uses; here the job is to remove it.
caution: Sap can cause a rash. Cutting alone makes it sprout aggressively; proper control is cut-stump herbicide or repeated pulling of seedlings. Learn to ID it so you do not kill native sumac or walnut by mistake.
lookalikes: Sumacs have toothed leaflets and red fruit. Black walnut has a chambered pith and round husked nuts. Tree-of-heaven leaflets are nearly untoothed except that one basal gland-tooth.

Ailanthus altissima ( ay-LAN-thəss al-TIH-sim-ə), commonly known as tree of heaven or ailanthus tree, is a deciduous tree in the quassia family. It is native to northeast, central China, and Taiwan. Unlike other members of the genus Ailanthus, it is found in temperate climates rather than the tropics.
The tree grows rapidly, and is capable of reaching heights of 15 metres (50 ft) in 25 years. While the species rarely lives more than 50 years, some specimens exceed 100 years of age. It is considered a noxious weed and vigorous invasive species, and one of the worst invasive plant species in Europe and North America. In 21st-century North America, the invasiveness of the species has been compounded by its role in the life cycle of the also destructive and invasive spotted lanternfly.

id_tips: Huge heart-shaped, fuzzy leaves (up to 2 ft on sprouts). Lavender foxglove-like flowers in spring before the leaves. Woody oval capsules persist in winter.
habitat: Roadsides, burns, landslides, and forest gaps. Native to China.
wnc: Invasive in the mountains; colonizes cliffs and disturbed forest after logging or fire.
uses: Valuable wood in Asia; here it is an invader. Flowers are showy, which is why it was planted.
caution: Produces millions of winged seeds. Do not plant.
lookalikes: Catalpa has similar big leaves but long bean-like pods and flowers with the leaves. Paulownia capsules are egg-shaped.
wikipedia_extract: Paulownia tomentosa, common names princess tree, empress tree, or foxglove-tree, is a deciduous hardwood tree in the family Paulowniaceae, native to central and eastern China and the Korean Peninsula. It is an extremely fast-growing tree with seeds that disperse readily and is considered an invasive exotic species in North America that has undergone naturalisation in large areas of the Eastern US, even though seed viability may be low under harsh conditions. P. tomentosa has also been introduced to Western and Central Europe, and is establishing itself as a naturalised species there as well.

id_tips: Ornamental pear. White flowers in early spring with a fishy smell. Glossy roundish leaves, scarlet fall color. Thorny wild-type offspring now form thickets. Small hard brown fruits.
habitat: Roadsides, old plantings, and spreading into fields and woods edges. Native to Asia.
wnc: NC Forest Service invasive tree. Bradford was the famous cultivar; its seedlings are worse.
uses: Was a popular street tree. Do not plant. Replace with serviceberry, dogwood, or native fringe tree.
caution: Weak branch crotches; Bradfords split in storms. Thorns on feral trees are serious.
lookalikes: Native serviceberry blooms about the same time but has five-petaled flowers that do not stink, and edible fruit.
wikipedia_extract: Pyrus calleryana, also known as the Callery pear, is a species of pear tree native to East Asia in the family Rosaceae. Its cultivar Bradford pear, known for its offensive odor that some have described as akin to "rotting fish", is widely planted throughout the United States and increasingly regarded as an invasive species.
image_credit: Photo via Wikipedia / Wikimedia Commons (File:Pyrus_calleryana.JPG). Used for local study.

id_tips: Shrub with silvery-scaled leaf undersides and stems. Fragrant pale-yellow flowers in spring. Speckled red berries in fall. Leaves are alternate.
habitat: Fields, roadsides, and forest edges. Planted for wildlife and mine reclamation, then escaped. Native to Asia.
wnc: One of the worst woody invasives in the mountains.
uses: Berries are edible and high in lycopene — a rare case of an invasive with a useful fruit. Eating the fruit does not control the plant (birds spread seeds). Nitrogen fixer that changes soil and shades out natives.
caution: Do not plant. If you eat berries, do not toss seeds in the woods. Thorny olive (E. pungens) is an evergreen relative, also invasive.
lookalikes: Native oleaster relatives are absent here. Buffalo berry is a western plant.
wikipedia_extract: Elaeagnus umbellata is a species of flowering plant known as Japanese silverberry, umbellata oleaster, autumn olive, autumn elaeagnus, spreading oleaster, autumnberry, or autumn berry. The species is indigenous to eastern Asia and ranges from the Himalayas eastwards to Japan. It is a hardy, aggressive invasive species able to readily colonize barren land, becoming invasive in the central and northeastern United States and parts of Europe.

id_tips: Arching, viciously thorny shrub. Many small white flowers in clusters. Leaves with a fringed, feathery stipule at the base (a key ID). Small red hips persist in winter.
habitat: Pastures, woods edges, and floodplains. Introduced from Asia as a living fence and for wildlife.
wnc: A NC-IPC / Forest Service invasive shrub. Forms impenetrable thickets.
uses: Hips are edible (as with most roses) but harvesting encourages you to walk into a thicket you should be removing. Native pasture rose (Rosa carolina) is the better plant.
caution: Thorns are nasty. Can harbor ticks.
lookalikes: Native roses have larger flowers, fewer in a cluster, and stipules that are not comb-fringed like this.
wikipedia_extract: Rosa multiflora (syn. Rosa polyantha) is a species of rose known commonly as multiflora rose, baby rose, Japanese rose, many-flowered rose, seven-sisters rose, Eijitsu rose and rambler rose. It is native to eastern Asia, in China, Japan, and Korea. It should not be confused with Rosa rugosa, which is also known as "Japanese rose", or with polyantha roses which are garden cultivars derived from hybrids of R. multiflora. It was introduced to North America, where it is an invasive species, forming extensive, impenetrable stands within forest understories, thickets, borders, and lowlands. It can be identified by its characteristic fringed stipules, which form pairs at the bases of leaf stalks bearing 3–89 leaves.

id_tips: Semi-evergreen shrub. Opposite leaves. Small white, sweet-smelling flower panicles in late spring, then dense clusters of dark berries. Often a wall of green along creeks.
habitat: Floodplains, woods edges, and abandoned yards. Native to China.
wnc: One of the most damaging shrubs in NC river bottoms and mountain valleys.
uses: Planted as a hedge. Berries feed birds, which is how it spreads. No recommended use; remove and replace with native viburnum or winterberry.
caution: Berries are toxic to people. Dense stands erase native understory.
lookalikes: Native viburnums have toothed leaves and different flower structure. Japanese privet has larger, glossier leaves.

id_tips: Twining vine. Opposite leaves. Fragrant white flowers that age to yellow, blooming for months. Black berries. Evergreen or semi-evergreen in WNC winters.
habitat: Fences, woods, fields — nearly every edge. Native to East Asia.
wnc: The most ubiquitous invasive vine in the region.
uses: Kids sip nectar from the flowers. That is the only benign use. It smothers trees and carpets the forest floor. Plant coral honeysuckle instead.
caution: Berries are not edible. Vines can girdle young trees.
lookalikes: Native coral honeysuckle has red tubular flowers and a fused leaf disk below the flower cluster.
wikipedia_extract: Lonicera japonica, known as Japanese honeysuckle and golden-and-silver honeysuckle, is a species of honeysuckle native to East Asia, including many parts of China. id_tips: Woody twining vine. Alternate round leaves. Flowers and orange-yellow capsules with red seeds are in small clusters along the stem (not just at the tips). Can climb and pull down mature trees.
habitat: Forest edges, roads, and interiors. Native to East Asia. Spread by people using the vines in fall wreaths.
wnc: A high-threat mountain invasive. Do not use in decorations.
uses: None. The pretty fruit is how it hitchhiked into wild forests. Native American bittersweet (Celastrus scandens) is uncommon and has fruit only in terminal clusters.
caution: Do not transport berrying vines. Fruit is poisonous to people.
lookalikes: American bittersweet has flowers/fruit in clusters only at the ends of twigs, and narrower leaves. When in doubt in WNC, it is almost always the invasive one.

id_tips: Evergreen vine. Juvenile leaves are 3–5 lobed; adult leaves on high flowering stems are unlobed. Dark berries on mature plants. Clings with adhesive roots.
habitat: Yards, woods near towns, and floodplains. Native to Europe.
wnc: A NC Cooperative Extension 'avoid' plant. Smothers trees and forest floors.
uses: A traditional ornamental groundcover — and a bad one. Berries feed some birds, which spread it. Native alternatives: green-and-gold, partridgeberry, Christmas fern.
caution: Berries and leaves are toxic. Sap can cause a rash. Heavy ivy can bring trees down in ice storms.
lookalikes: Juvenile poison ivy is deciduous and has 3 leaflets, not evergreen lobed ivy leaves.
