Hedera helix, simply ivy, or common ivy, English ivy, European ivy, King's choice ivy, is a species of flowering plant in the family Araliaceae. It is native to most of Europe and parts of western Asia. Ivy is a clinging evergreen vine that grows on tree trunks, walls, and fences in gardens, waste spaces, and wild habitats. Ivy is common as an ornamental plant, but escaped plants become naturalised outside its native range. Ivy has considerable cultural significance and symbolism.
Synonyms include Hedera acuta, Hedera arborea ('tree ivy'), Hedera baccifera, and Hedera grandifolia. Other common names are bindwood and lovestone.

id_tips: A delicate annual grass. Leaves have a faint silvery midrib. Grows in dense mats 1–3 ft tall. Weak, sprawling stems that look like they are on stilts. Seeds in late summer–fall.
habitat: Floodplains, trails, logging roads, and shaded lawns. Native to Asia; likely arrived as packing material.
wnc: One of the worst forest-floor invasives in the mountains. Spreads on boots and mowers.
uses: None. Pull before it seeds. Native river oats and sedges belong in those wet woods instead.
caution: A single plant can drop hundreds of seeds that last years in the soil. Clean boots after hiking through it.
lookalikes: White grass (Leersia virginica) is a native that lacks the silver midrib and does not form the same choking mats.

id_tips: Bamboo-like hollow stems with red nodes, but it is not a bamboo. Broad, somewhat triangular leaves. Sprays of tiny white flowers in late summer. Dies to the ground in winter, leaving cane-like stalks.
habitat: Creek banks, roads, and waste ground. Native to East Asia.
wnc: A high-threat invasive, especially along mountain rivers. Extremely hard to kill.
uses: Young spring shoots are edible (like sour rhubarb) in its native range and among foragers. Eating it does not control it. Roots are used in some herbal products (resveratrol); that market has encouraged planting — a bad idea here.
caution: Never dump stems or roots; tiny fragments resprout. Do not plant. Control usually needs a multi-year plan.
lookalikes: Giant knotweed is even larger. Native knotweeds are much smaller and not cane-forming.
wikipedia_extract: Reynoutria japonica, synonyms Fallopia japonica and Polygonum cuspidatum, is a species of herbaceous perennial plant in the knotweed and buckwheat family Polygonaceae. Common names include Japanese knotweed and Asian knotweed. It is native to East Asia in Japan, China and Korea. In North America and Europe, the species has successfully established itself in numerous habitats; it is classified as a pest and invasive species in several countries. The plant is popular with beekeepers and its young stems are edible, making it an increasingly popular foraged vegetable with a flavour described as lemony rhubarb.

id_tips: Biennial. Year-1: a low rosette of kidney-shaped, scalloped leaves. Year-2: a 1–4 ft stalk with triangular toothed leaves, small white four-petaled flowers, and skinny seed pods. Crushed leaves smell of garlic.
habitat: Floodplain forests, trails, and campgrounds. Native to Europe.
wnc: Invading mountain woods; especially bad in rich coves. It also poisons soil fungi that native trees need.
uses: Edible — leaves are a garlic-mustard green, high in vitamins. Pulling and eating (or bagging) before seed is actually useful control if you get the root. Do not compost seed-bearing plants.
caution: Wash greens from clean sites. Do not let it go to seed. One plant can spread thousands of seeds.
lookalikes: Violets and ground ivy can look like the rosette; neither smells strongly of garlic when crushed, and neither bolts into a mustard stalk.

id_tips: Small shrub with tiny spoon-shaped leaves, usually in clusters, and a single sharp spine at each node. Yellow inner bark. Red berries hang along the stems. Cultivars may be burgundy.
habitat: Yards, then woods. Native to Japan. Still sold in some nurseries.

id_tips: Shrub with corky, winged ridges on the stems. Opposite leaves that turn screaming scarlet in fall. Orange-red fruit capsules.
habitat: Old plantings spreading into woods. Native to Asia.
wnc: NC-IPC shun list. Still common in landscaping.
uses: Fall color is why it was planted. Native hearts-a-bustin', fothergilla, and blackgum give fall color without invading.
caution: Fruit is poisonous. Birds spread it into forests.
lookalikes: Native strawberry-bush (hearts-a-bustin') has green four-sided stems without corky wings.

Euonymus alatus, known variously as burning bush, winged euonymus, winged spindle, and winged spindle-tree, is a species of flowering plant in the family Celastraceae, native to central and northern China, Japan, and Korea.
It is a popular ornamental plant in gardens and parks due to its bright pink or orange fruit and attractive autumn color: The common name "burning bush" refers to its bright red autumn color. The cultivars 'Compactus' and 'Fire Ball' have gained the Royal Horticultural Society's Award of Garden Merit.

id_tips: Woody clockwise-twining vine (Chinese) with hanging clusters of violet pea flowers in spring, usually before leaves. Pinnate leaves. Heavy, rope-like trunks can girdle trees. Japanese wisteria (W. floribunda) is also invasive and twines counterclockwise.
habitat: Old home sites, roads, and woods. Native to Asia.
wnc: Listed invasive vine. Native American wisteria (Wisteria frutescens) is the one to plant instead — it blooms later, on new wood, and is much less aggressive.
uses: Ornamental flowers. All wisterias have toxic seeds and pods.
caution: Seeds are poisonous. Vines can take down mature trees. Do not dump trimmings in the woods.
lookalikes: Native American wisteria has shorter flower clusters and blooms with or after the leaves.
wikipedia_extract: Wisteria sinensis, commonly known as the Chinese wisteria, is a species of flowering plant in the pea family, native to China, in the provinces of Guangxi, Guizhou, Hebei, Henan, Hubei, Shaanxi, and Yunnan. Growing 20–30 m (66–98 ft) tall, it is a deciduous vine. It is widely cultivated in temperate regions for its twisting stems and masses of scented flowers in hanging racemes, in spring.

id_tips: Not a bamboo. Evergreen shrub with twice- or thrice-compound leaves that often blush red in winter. White flower panicles, then clusters of bright red berries.
habitat: Yards and nearby woods. Native to East Asia.
wnc: On the NC-IPC shun list. Birds spread berries into forests.
uses: A landscaping plant. Berries are toxic to cedar waxwings (documented die-offs). Replace with native winterberry or Virginia sweetspire.
caution: Cyanogenic berries — do not use in holiday decorations where pets or children might eat them, and do not plant where waxwings flock.
lookalikes: True bamboo has jointed hollow canes and no red berry clusters like this.

Nandina domestica ( nan-DEE-nə) commonly known as nandina, heavenly bamboo or sacred bamboo, is a species of flowering plant in the family Berberidaceae, native to eastern Asia from the Himalayas to Japan. It is the only member of the monotypic genus Nandina. Despite its name, it is not a true bamboo.
Nandina is widely grown in gardens as an ornamental plant with a number of cultivars that display bright-red fall foliage in the cool months, and attractive new foliage growth in spring. Although a popular ornamental shrub, the berries are toxic to birds, especially towards the end of the winter when other food sources become scarce.

id_tips: Evergreen trailing groundcover. Opposite shiny leaves. Five-petaled violet-blue flowers in spring. Forms a dense mat that excludes everything else. Vinca major is a larger-leaved relative, also invasive.
habitat: Old homesteads, graveyards, and woods near towns. Native to Europe.
wnc: Cooperative Extension lists vinca as an exotic to avoid. Still sold as a groundcover.
uses: A traditional graveyard and yard plant. Alkaloids from related Vinca/Catharanthus species are used in chemotherapy drugs — that is industrial pharmacy, not a reason to plant it here.
caution: Toxic if eaten. Smothers native spring ephemerals. Replace with green-and-gold, foamflower, or partridgeberry.
lookalikes: Native phloxes have different leaves and are not evergreen mats like this.

id_tips: Arching shrub with long pointed, pale-backed leaves. Conical spikes of tiny purple (or white/pink) fragrant flowers in summer. Seeds copiously.
habitat: Roadsides, river gravel, and old gardens. Native to China.
wnc: NC-IPC shun list. Invades mountain riverbanks and burns.
uses: Adult butterflies nectar on it, which is why it was planted — but it is not a host plant for native caterpillars, so it is junk food in the landscape. Plant native Joe-Pye, bee balm, and milkweed instead.
caution: Do not plant. Deadhead does not solve the invasion in WNC rivers.
lookalikes: Native summer-blooming spikes like liatris are herbaceous, not woody shrubs.

Buddleja davidii (spelling variant Buddleia davidii), also called butterfly-bush, orange eye, or summer lilac, is a species of flowering plant in the family Scrophulariaceae, native to most of China except for the far northeast. It is widely used as an ornamental plant, and many named cultivars are in cultivation. The genus was named Buddleja after the English botanist, Reverend Adam Buddle. The species name, davidii, is after the French missionary and explorer in China, Father Armand David, who was the first European to report the shrub. It was found near Yichang by Dr Augustine Henry about 1887 and sent to St Petersburg. Another botanist-missionary in China, Jean-André Soulié, sent seed to the French nursery Vilmorin, and B. davidii entered commerce in the 1890s.
B. davidii was accorded the RHS Award of Merit (AM) in 1898, and the Award of Garden Merit (AGM) in 1941.

id_tips: Tall clumping ornamental grass, 4–8 ft. Feathery fan-shaped plumes in late summer. Leaves with a pale midrib. Spreads from plantings into roadsides and woods edges.
habitat: Yards, then roadsides, powerlines, and disturbed slopes. Native to East Asia.
wnc: NC Forest Service invasive grass. Also a fire hazard when dry.
uses: A landscaping grass. Native alternatives: big bluestem, Indian grass, switchgrass, river oats.
caution: Highly flammable in winter. Do not dump yard waste in the woods.
lookalikes: Native plumegrasses and bluestems have different seed heads; miscanthus plumes are the classic ornamental-grass look.
wikipedia_extract: Miscanthus sinensis, also called eulalia grass, Chinese silver grass, or elephant grass, is a species of flowering plant in the grass family Poaceae, native to most of East Asia (China, Japan, Taiwan and Korea) and Southeast Asia (the Philippines, eastern Indonesia, Malaysia, Vietnam, Thailand, and Laos).

id_tips: Three leaflets ('leaves of three, let it be'). The end leaflet has a longer stalk than the two side ones. Can be a groundcover, a shrub, or a hairy-rooted vine up trees. Small whitish berries. Often reddish when new.
habitat: Edges, woods, floodplains, and yards. A native plant — not invasive, but essential to know.
wnc: Extremely common. Included so you do not mix it up with Virginia creeper, boxelder seedlings, or fragrant sumac.
uses: Berries are a high-fat food for many birds. Deer browse it. Native, ecologically useful — and a rash factory for most people. Not a plant you cultivate on purpose.
caution: Urushiol oil causes the rash; it stays active on clothes, tools, and dead vines for a long time. Do not burn (smoke can blister lungs). Jewelweed is the traditional wash; washing with soap as soon as possible is the proven first step.
lookalikes: Virginia creeper has five leaflets. Boxelder seedlings have three leaflets but opposite leaves and no vine hairs. Fragrant sumac has three leaflets but the end leaflet is not on a long stalk.

Toxicodendron radicans, commonly known as eastern poison ivy or poison ivy, is a species of allergenic flowering plant. It has numerous subtaxons and forms both vines and shrubs. Despite its common name, it is not a true ivy, but rather a member of the cashew and sumac family, Anacardiaceae. It is different from western poison ivy, Toxicodendron rydbergii, and resembles a number of species.
The species is found in North America. Although commonly eaten by animals, with birds consuming the seeds, T. radicans is considered a noxious weed. As a poison ivy, it causes urushiol-induced contact dermatitis in most people who touch it, producing an itchy, irritating, and sometimes painful rash.
